Commentary.Commentary: The action now shifts to Ahmedabad, where one hopes the air will stay clear and the focus firmly on cricket. It is the finale of South Africa's tour, with a chance still alive for them to level the series and head home smiling. India, though, will have their sights set on a 3-1 finish, to go with the 2-1 ODI series win, even if it may not fully erase the disappointment of losing a home Test series. The fifth T20I will be played on Friday, 19 December 2025, starting at 7 pm IST (1.30 pm GMT). Do join us early for the build-up. Thanks for your company, goodbye and cheers!

What an uneventful evening it turned out to be. There was plenty of hope, followed by heartbreak for those who made the trip to the ground. They waited patiently and cheered every umpire inspection, only to head home with a 'foggy memory' of the night. Unfortunate, as it gets.

At around 6.30 pm IST, Robin Uthappa, speaking on air, had suggested that delaying the start would be counterintuitive, with the fog only set to thicken as the evening rolls on. Those words proved prophetic and, inevitably, the fourth T20I got abandoned, without a toss and after six inspections from the umpires. From here on, India cannot lose the series, meaning their purple patch in bilateral contests since the 2024 T20 World Cup continues.

Fog, air pollution and cricket, an uncomfortable trio coming together. When visibility drops and the air turns heavy, the game is no longer just about bat and ball but about safety, stamina and perhaps, common sense. Tonight, patience runs out as reality steps in, and the only sensible call is made. The wait is over, and the MATCH HAS BEEN CALLED OFF.

UPDATE - 9.26 pm IST (3.56 pm GMT) - Out come the two umpires for the inspection. Hopeful eyes await, and whenever Rohan Pandit and KN Ananthapadmanabhan have made their way out, they are greeted by a loud cheer from the crowd who have gone nowhere. The two umpires stand at either end of the 22 yards and look into the distance to check the visibility. A few of the Indian players have been spotted on the balcony. Another inspection in the offing?

UPDATE - 8.59 pm IST (3.29 pm GMT) - Inspection time, the 5th of the night, if you are wondering. What has been the practice so far is for the two umpires to walk around the outfield to assess the visibility and whether they can see into the distance before moving towards the strip. This time, they have gone straight onto the pitch, which is still covered with the hessian cloth. They are now seen relaying their observations to representatives of the Indian camp. And the wait continues, we will have one more inspection at 9.25 pm IST. Mayanti Langer shares on air that 9.46 pm IST is the cut-off time for a five-over contest, but we are yet to receive official confirmation.

In case you missed it, following their win in the previous match in Dharamsala, India now hold the record for the most wins against South Africa in T20Is, taking the tally to 20 in 34 meetings. The second team after India to beat South Africa the most in this format is Australia, with 19 wins out of 28 played. Interestingly, when it comes to South Africa, the team they have beaten the most in T20Is is India. The Proteas achieved this milestone with their win in Mullanpur, surpassing Australia and England, who have beaten India 12 times. Their tally now stands at 13 victories in 34 matches.

UPDATE - 8.29 pm IST (2.59 pm GMT) - Out come the two most important people at the moment on the ground - Rohan Pandit and KN Ananthapadmanabhan. The crowd gives them a big cheer, in hope! The umpires are scanning every angle of the ground. Rajeev Shukla, the vice-president of the BCCI, is also in the middle, in conversation with the match officials. One of the umpires flashes a thumbs-up. Is that a hint of positive news on the way? The spectators are flashing their mobile lights. And here comes the verdict... another inspection scheduled for 9 pm IST.

Fog in the air, a wet ball, it is shaping up as a unique challenge. Eyes and hands will be put through a stern test in the field, and player safety will rightly remain the top priority for the officials. With plenty of cricket coming up in the days ahead, the last thing anyone wants is an injury, so all we can do now is wait for the next inspection, which could well be the final call if conditions do not improve. It is hard to see how things will improve, though. Science suggests that as the night goes on, the fog only gets denser, making the wait feel more like hope than certainty.

UPDATE - 7.59 pm IST (2.29 pm GMT) - The umpires stride out and take a slow walk along the boundary, carefully checking the visibility as the moment of truth edges closer. Now, they head towards the middle. Both officials are trying their best to check every angle of the ground, it's a big decision to make. The crowd watches on with bated breath. Are we seeing a handshake? Nopes. NEXT INSPECTION WILL BE AT 8.30 PM IST. FYI... the pitch is being covered!

UPDATE - 7.54 pm IST (2.24 pm GMT) - Is that a hint of good news? The ground staff are out there rolling the pitch, perhaps to deal with the dew that has settled in. That said, the real concern remains the fog, and all eyes will be on the umpires at 8 pm IST, which is not too far away now.

What is an Ashes Test without a day of drama, right? Alex Carey went on to score his maiden Ashes century, once again proving his value for Australia under pressure. However, what emerged after the close of play will not please the tourists. There was a caught behind appeal when Carey was on 72. After it was turned down on-field, England reviewed. While there was a noise and a spike on Snicko, it appeared to occur before the ball was anywhere near the bat, and the on-field call was upheld. Carey later admitted he heard a noise and felt there may have been a feather. BBG Sports, the provider of the Snicko technology, has since issued a statement. They said that based on Carey’s admission, the only conclusion is that the Snicko operator at the time must have selected the incorrect stump microphone for audio processing. Bizarre.

UPDATE - 7.32 pm IST (2.02 pm GMT) - It’s time for the second inspection. The two umpires are assessing visibility whilst standing at either end of the ground to check whether they can spot each other from a distance. We are hearing that another inspection will take place at 8 pm IST. Dale Steyn shares on air that around 8 pm IST last night, visibility was even worse than this, and he wasn't able to see anything. It is not promising at the moment, but let’s hope for the best.

Air quality has been a hot topic across India, and Lucknow is no exception. Fog hangs in the air, and the AQI was last recorded above 400, conditions that are far from ideal, especially for athletes. It brings back memories of the 2017 Delhi Test, when poor air forced Sri Lankan players to wear masks, and the situation got so grim that trainer Nick Lee even pulled on his whites to make up the eleven. Let us see what this evening has in store.

Kuldeep Yadav is up for a chat. He says it was a good outing for him in the last game and, with it being his birthday, felt it was a special day where he was able to create some magic. He adds that it was very important for the team to win that game and take the series lead. Kuldeep jokes that when a team is struggling and is 7 or 8 wickets down, that’s when you want to be bowling the 20th over, not when they have only lost one or two wickets. Reckons that this will be a good wicket to bat on. On switching formats, he says moving from red-ball cricket to white-ball formats is relatively easy, but the transition from T20s to Test cricket is much more difficult and requires time in between to adjust. Further says that in ODIs and T20s, a lot of the game is about playing with the field positions, which is particularly challenging in ODIs with four fielders allowed outside the 30-yard circle for the most part. Mentions that they had a very good net session yesterday, and while they know the conditions here well, he feels the main challenges will be dealing with the dew and visibility.

UPDATE - 6.55 pm IST (1.25 pm GMT) - The umpires have relayed their observations to both teams, and the fog remains too heavy for play at the moment. Another inspection will take place at 7.30 pm IST.

Following Ashes? Only yesterday, there was talk that Usman Khawaja's Test career was all but done. Destiny had other plans. Steven Smith's sudden bout of dizziness forced him out, opened the door, and the left-hander walked in to script a timely 82, reminding everyone that class never really checks out. The star of day one in Adelaide, though, was Alex Carey (106). Batting with flair and fearlessness, he stitched vital stands with the lower order to rescue Australia from a wobbly 94 for 4. England bowled reasonably well, but the fielding told a different story. Jofra Archer, though, was pure theatre, breathing fire and picking up three red-hot wickets. Australia have closed on 326 for 8 in a Test nicely poised, with the next two days expected to be kinder to batting. Eyes are split between Adelaide and Lucknow, where we are just minutes away from the inspection.

Update - 6.33 pm IST (1.03 pm GMT) - The toss has been delayed thanks to a blanket of fog, with the white ball proving hard to spot. An inspection is scheduled for 6.50 pm IST, so for now it is a waiting game with fingers crossed and eyes on the sky. Robin Uthappa, speaking on air, makes a valid point. He feels delaying the start could be a counterintuitive call, with the fog likely to thicken rather than clear as the evening wears on.

Pitch report - Deep Dasgupta is pitchside alongside Pommie Mbangwa. Deep notes that the square boundaries measure 66 metres on either side, with 76 metres straight down the ground. Informs that the surface is a mix of red and black soil. Pommie adds that the surface with this soil mixture usually holds together nicely and offers consistent bounce. Mentions that the pitch is very cold at the moment, and regardless of whether there is moisture in it, it is difficult to keep the cold out of the surface. Further shares that it was last watered a couple of days ago and is expected to remain cold, which means it’s unlikely to be as high-scoring as we often see in the IPL. Believes that a total in the region of 160 to 170 will be competitive.

Did you know? Win rate batting first in T20Is at Bharat Ratna Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee Ekana Cricket Stadium reads impressively at 83.33 percent with five wins and just one loss. But with dew looming, the toss becomes a tricky call. Do you stick to history or read the conditions on the day? That is the question both captains will be pondering.

The last T20I international at this venue was back in 2023, when New Zealand were folded for 99 on a slow and low track. In reply, it was a real grind for India, who chased the target with just one ball to spare. The pitch came under criticism from all quarters, but a lot of water has passed under the bridge since then. Earlier this year, in the IPL, the last three night games here saw 200-plus scores being racked up in 5 out of the 6 innings. All of which sets the stage for an intriguing contest. Stay tuned for the toss and team news.

As for South Africa, their batting unit has struggled throughout the white-ball leg whenever the ball has moved around. Frequent chopping and changing in this series appears to have done more harm than good. Quinton de Kock, Aiden Markram and David Miller, who have previously represented Lucknow in the IPL, will have a better understanding of the conditions, and we could see Miller returning to the side. On the bowling front, their quicks will want to replicate the way they hit their straps early in Mullanpur after spraying it around in the last game.

India have been heavily reliant on Abhishek Sharma, and it was his fireworks that allowed the hosts to break the back of the chase early in Dharamsala. With 7 T20Is remaining, including this fixture, before the World Cup, there continues to be concern around the form of Suryakumar Yadav and his deputy Shubman Gill, though SKY has reiterated that he is out of runs, not out of form. One of the positives in the bowling department from the last win was the way Arshdeep Singh stepped up after a tough outing, combining well with Harshit Rana in the absence of Jasprit Bumrah.

Hello and a warm welcome, everyone! The T20I series began in Cuttack and has since travelled north. We have now arrived at the final stop of that journey here in Lucknow, with India currently 2-1 up, before the action moves to Ahmedabad for the final game. Will the series still be alive by then? We will find out over the next few hours.
... MATCH DAY ...

Lucknow, a city celebrated for its 'nafasat aur nazakat', steps forward to host cricket's naughtiest format, a game that cares little for delicacy or subtlety. With the five-match T20I series already tilted in India's favour, South Africa are in no position to say 'pehle aap'. That famed gesture of courtesy here would simply hand the hosts an unassailable lead, an invitation the visitors can ill afford to extend. Across the three games so far, South Africa's batting has been inconsistent, to put it mildly, veering between the sublime and the ridiculous. Dew has been a decisive factor for both sides. In the second game, the Proteas showed the way by piling up a big total and then staying disciplined with the ball under trying conditions. The same template was required at Dharamsala, but they could not replicate it as the surface suddenly assisted the pacers, offering lateral movement. On that count, going in without a frontline spinner was a smart call, but the meek surrender from the batters left the pace battery with too little in reserve to mount a serious fight. As many as three changes were made by the touring side in the last game, and with the series on the line, it will be intriguing to see the combination they back in Lucknow, where dew could once again play a telling role as winter begins to set in. India have played three T20Is at this venue and remain unbeaten, a statistic that will only bolster their confidence after a commanding win in the third T20I. Without Jasprit Bumrah and Axar Patel, the bowling initially appeared to be the softer side of their game, especially after what unfolded at Mullanpur. But Arshdeep Singh silenced the doubters, made full use of the conditions, and scripted a fine redemption story. If one were to nitpick, the Indian batting during the last chase was far from convincing in testing conditions. Had Abhishek Sharma not seized the initiative in the Powerplay, it could easily have drifted into a close finish. With Axar ruled out and Bumrah unlikely to return, India are expected to stick with the last winning XI. Although Shubman Gill and Suryakumar Yadav are yet to hit top gear, the hosts will hope those gears finally click in the capital city, a place rich in history and culture, where timing, like good manners, is everything, and form, much like tradition, eventually finds its way back.
